population.note: Six chapters (Region and Regional Development; Geography: Nature and Scope; Population Part 2; Population Part 1; Human Settlements and Land Use; Primary Economic Activities), 2026-09-24. RECALL IS UNMEASURABLE FOR THIS LANE AND THE PROBE SAYS SO ('n/a'): no chapter has an attached figure, so there is no known-positive population to measure the rule against and the flagged count is a FLOOR. All 72 hits are SELFCONTAINED, which is a property of THIS BOOK'S GRAPHICS rather than luck: concept maps, skill charts, a job advertisement, a pictogram, labelled pie and bar charts, shape-only population pyramids, and choropleth maps whose whole content is a legend plus place labels. None is an image a reader must MEASURE, so a transcription can inline it completely. TWO ROWS ARE PHOTOGRAPHS and they are the weak cases: Population Part 1's fig. 1.5 satellite pair and Human Settlements' fig. 3.1 valley photo. Both are answerable from their described context, but the description is a reading rather than a transcription, so these are the rows where attaching the image would genuinely add something. THE PROBE READS `context`, NOT ONLY `text`: most of these rows have stems with no figure word at all and were flagged through the shared set context. Note also that Human Settlements' two Land Use Land Cover map activities did NOT flag, because their stems name no figure - so the probe's count here is a floor in that direction as well. ONE ACTIVITY WAS DELIBERATELY NOT INGESTED for figure reasons: Ch.3's fig. 3.2 asks the student to match six satellite photographs to six named settlement patterns. Describing each photograph in the stem would state the very characteristic the student is asked to identify, so inlining it destroys the question rather than preserving it. Ch.4, Ch.5 and Ch.6 carry 'On an outline map of the world, show the following' questions (DRAWS, not MISS) and 'study the map above and answer' questions over real choropleths, which are the lane's first genuine MISS candidates.

rows.why: 'Go through the Regional Imbalance Reduction Strategy chart (fig. 7.2) and write two sentences on each factor' keeps the book's figure citation, but the chart's ENTIRE content is reproduced in the stem directly beneath it: both branches (Provision of Public Goods/Services, Provision of Infrastructure and Stimulus) and all eleven leaf factors, transcribed off the rendered page. Fig. 7.2 is a concept map, not a data graphic - it carries no values, no scale and no legend, so the labels ARE the figure. A student can answer it in full from the text alone. This is the class the probe's own 26% measured precision is made of: a figure CITATION is not a figure DEPENDENCE. The citation was deliberately kept rather than stripped, because it is the row's provenance back to the printed page, and stripping it would change the stem and therefore the content_hash of an already-committed row.

'Make a list of the skills obtained through the study of Geography ... (fig. 8.1, Skills of a Geographer)' keeps the citation, and the stem then lists all nine skills the figure contains. Fig. 8.1 is a labelled spider chart with no data, no scale and no picture - its labels ARE its content, and they are reproduced verbatim. Answerable in full from the text.

'A newspaper item listing job opportunities is given below (fig. 8.5, Sample Advertisement)' - all seven advertisements are transcribed into the stem, each with its post, qualifications, experience and post count. Fig. 8.5 is a rasterised clipping of TEXT, so nothing is lost by inlining it. Note this figure is also the reason the chapter needs a figtext.json: its glyphs carry the +29 cmap offset documented in config.ts, so the text layer renders it as '8QLRQ3XEOLF6HUYLFH' and it had to be read off the rendered page.

One of six set members sharing a `context` that describes fig. 3.1, an aerial photograph of a glaciated valley, point by point: A on a bare snow-patched mountain slope, B on a vegetated hill slope, C on the flat valley floor, D on sandy ground at the water's edge, E on flat green land beside the braided river. Every one of the six questions asks WHERE a settlement would or would not develop and why, so what the question needs from the photograph is the terrain at each lettered point, and that is stated. Classified SELFCONTAINED alongside Population Part 1's fig. 1.5, and with the same caveat: this is a PHOTOGRAPH, so the description is a reading of it rather than a transcription of printed labels. A student answering from the text is trusting that reading. It is the honest verdict because the question is answerable, but these photograph rows are the two places in this lane where attaching the image would add something a description cannot.

One of 33 set members whose shared `context` transcribes fig. 4.1, the world map of major regions of primary activities: its five-class index with the colour of each class, the latitude lines, every named ocean, sea and fishing bank, and the distribution of each class continent by continent. The questions ask which activities appear where, in which latitudes, and which continent lacks one - all of them readable off that description. This is the lane's largest single figure dependence and the one whose inlining took most care, because the map is a DISTRIBUTION map rather than a labelled diagram: what it carries is the position of shaded areas and symbols, not printed values. The context therefore states the distribution at the grain the questions ask (continent, coast, latitude band) and no finer, so that nothing in an answer rests on a reading the description does not support.
